We investigate two doubly enriched hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) compositions, h10B15N and h11B15N, to determine how isotope substitution on both sublattices modifies mid-infrared hyperbolic phonon polaritons (HPhPs). Polarization-resolved room temperature and cryogenic far-field reflectance measurements reveal optical-phonon blue shifts of approximately 35 cm-1 in h10B15N relative h11B15N, translating both Reststrahlen bands (RBs) and their polariton dispersions. For the upper RB, the combined accessible range expands from 1360-1614 cm-1 in natural hBN to 1356-1640 cm-1 across the B- enriched 14N crystals and 1339-1640 cm-1 when the 15N enriched crystals are included. Near-field imaging confirms deeply sub-diffractional propagation and shows that both crystals exhibit lower polariton damping and longer lifetimes than natural hBN, with performance comparable to monoisotopically enriched crystals. Further, we compare the conventional reduced-mass description with a phenomenological two-component inverse-mass model that captures the isotope dependence of the phonon frequencies and LO-TO coupling while resolving the contributions of the individual sublattices. These results establish multicomponent isotope engineering as a materials design strategy for positioning the HPhPs spectral range while preserving low-loss propagation in polar vdW crystals.

papers.title: From oscillations to symmetry breaking in a two-dimensional piecewise-smooth dynamical system
papers.abstract: We propose a discrete-time dynamical model in which two players, each distributed over two positions, interact only at the positions of their maximal presence, with an intensity set by an external resource. The main idea is that the evolution of the maxima closes into a self-contained two-dimensional piecewise-smooth map that can be analysed exactly. We show that a single critical level of the resource separates two outcomes: below it, the players exchange leadership forever along a stable cycle; above it, the symmetry between them breaks, and an arbitrarily small initial advantage grows into a permanent winner--loser hierarchy. The local stability of these regimes is proved, and their global attractivity is supported by numerical experiments. At the critical level itself, all dominance is erased and both players end in equal division of the resource. Mathematically, the transition is a border-collision bifurcation shaped by this symmetry.

papers.title: Impact of compressiblity approximations on atmospheric gravity wave characteristics
papers.abstract: Atmospheric gravity waves are a common phenomenon in the atmosphere and are of critical importance to understanding power generation from wind plants. Common sources of atmospheric gravity waves are stratified flow over topography or wind deceleration ahead of wind farms. Simulations to understand atmospheric boundary layer conditions and wind power generation often solve the Navier-Stokes equations in incompressible Boussinesq form, which allows for density variation as a function of potential temperature only; the purpose of this study is to understand how much that simplification matters. In this work, we evaluate simulated internal gravity wave characteristics by modeling stratified flow over bell-shaped hills using three forms of the governing equations: the linearized incompressible Boussinesq form, the full incompressible Boussinesq form, and the fully compressible form. While all formulations predict qualitatively similar wave structures, the compressible equations predict larger parcel displacements at higher altitudes, higher variations in apparent wavelengths, and more differences in wave angle, particularly at low Froude numbers. These differences can be attributed to compressibility and non-linear effects. The physical implications of differing wave characteristics become especially important in low Froude number regimes. These differences can, in turn, lead to differing predictions of wind farm performance and the characteristics of wind farm-induced gravity waves, underscoring the potential importance of compressibility effects in accurately capturing flow behavior in strongly stratified environments.

papers.title: A probabilistic model of visual segmentation explains early visual cortical dynamics
papers.abstract: Neural dynamics are a central feature of biological neural systems. In the visual cortex, the functional role of neural dynamics is poorly understood, particularly for static stimuli. The statistics of still natural images have long been used by models that successfully predict firing in early visual cortex; those models assume that neurons represent inferences about latent image features, but often ignore the dynamics of said inference. Here, we test if inferential dynamics in images explain visual-cortical dynamics. To do so, we present a biologically plausible model of cortical computation which assumes that the inference of features is coupled with inference about how those features are organized into meaningful parts, a function also known as segmentation. Given an input image, our model iterates between inferring the features and the segments, through recurrence and feedback, thus inducing dynamics in the neural representation of features. For these neural dynamics, we derive theoretical and exact predictions. Our model predicts both gain and variability in evoked responses to natural images, and we show that it captures classical single-neuron experimental findings such as gain dynamics and variability decay during stimulus presentation. The model also predicts that those dynamics are organized around inferred segment structure and more heterogeneous than previously thought, reflecting the complexity of inference for natural scenes. Finally, our analytical formulation provides a clear interpretation of our results. Insights from our normative model could generalize to segmentation problems in other experimental modalities, and help address the cost of inference in artificial networks with iterative computation.

papers.title: Early State Exclusion for $5\times5$ Jacobi Matrices
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present a problem that arose from quantum computing, when the quantum state to be transferred completely vanishes before the first occurrence of the perfect state transfer. It was posed as an open problem for 1D quantum chains with $n$ of qubits, where $n>4$ is an odd number. We present the solution for $n=5$. The proofs are accessible to students who studied trigonometry and calculus. As for the set-up the knowledge of eigentheory and inner products from linear algebra is needed.

papers.title: Chemotactic recruitment offsets congestion in honeybee trophallaxis
papers.abstract: Honeybee colonies distribute food by trophallaxis, a sequence of local interactions in which nectar donors transfer resources to hungry nestmates. Efficient transfer requires a searcher to find a donor and then be served. Chemical signals may draw searchers to a donor, though the crowd they form may block the way. We develop a stochastic framework coupling velocity-jump search that depends on chemical signaling to random-order service at donor aggregations, and measure trophallactic efficiency by the time the colony needs to feed a prescribed fraction of its members. Directed recruitment emerges because fed bees linger near donors and strengthen local chemical cues, but lingering also slows service. Trophallactic efficiency is therefore maximized at an intermediate abandonment rate that balances recruitment against congestion. We determine when displaced cues remain useful and how competing donors partition searchers. With two donors of unequal service rate, the faster one produces fed bees sooner and so advertises more strongly, drawing recruitment toward the donor that can sustain more throughput and away from the one that would congest. Together, these results show how feedback between service and signaling can self-organize recruitment to match local service capacity without centralized coordination.

papers.title: Instrumental variables with treatment clusters
papers.abstract: Many policy evaluations include multiple unordered treatments. A common approach is to aggregate these treatments into clusters and apply instrumental variable (IV) methods at the treatment cluster level: The clusters are treated as binary treatments and the IV assumptions are invoked at the cluster level. This paper shows that IV with treatment clusters identifies a weighted average of local average treatment effects (LATEs) under a set of assumptions at the unclustered treatment level. When data on unclustered treatment choice is available, we propose testable necessary conditions for the causal interpretation of IV with treatment clusters. We illustrate our methods with empirical applications to the causal effects of fields of study aggregated into STEM and non-STEM clusters or eight broad study directions.

papers.title: Towards Scalable Network-Based Interventions for HIV Treatment and Prevention via R2C-Agent
papers.abstract: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) remains a pressing public health challenge worldwide. Targeting limited HIV prevention and treatment resources effectively with network-based algorithms is a long-standing problem with a rich history at AAMAS and other computational venues. However, optimizing targeted biomedical interventions for minimizing spread of HIV often requires observability of the contact network of HIV transmission risk behavior among individuals, which is prohibitively expensive to collect at scale. Peer referral networks, i.e., networks collected through a recursive peer referral process, are an alternative network class often used to study HIV in hidden populations that can be collected digitally at scale, but they deviate from the underlying contact network: referrals can follow non-risk social ties and participants accept only one referral, hiding contacts among already-recruited individuals. In this work, we first formalize the novel problem of planning network-based interventions to minimize HIV spread in the hidden contact network while observing only the peer referral network. Second, we implement R2C-Agent, a decision making agent for interventions that is designed around our new conditional graph diffusion model called Referral-to-Contact Diffusion (R2C-Diff). R2C-Diff positions the peer referral process as incremental corruption of the underlying contact network and learns to reverse it. R2C-Agent plans its interventions over contact networks sampled from R2C-Diff, so its decisions account for uncertainty about the hidden contact network. Finally, we conduct simulated experiments using real-world HIV network data that demonstrate that R2C-Agent empirically plans more effective interventions than baselines from interdisciplinary literature and highlight key tradeoffs and assumptions driving performance.

papers.title: One Trajectory, Two Requirements: Accuracy and Local Stability in Euler Sampling for Flow Matching Policies
papers.abstract: Flow matching robot policies commonly use a fixed Euler step count selected from offline accuracy sweeps. At inference time, however, each policy input (visual observation, robot state, and language instruction) together with a source-noise draw defines a different ODE trajectory and sequence of local Jacobians. We ask whether a step count that accurately follows the nominal noise-to-action trajectory can still be too coarse for strongly contracting directions around it. An exact two-coordinate system and a controlled augmentation of six trained flow models show that trajectory accuracy and local Euler stability can impose different step requirements even when the original learned transport is unchanged. We then study a frozen $π_{0.5}$-LIBERO checkpoint without modifying its weights or action dynamics. Across 30 policy inputs from 10 LIBERO-10 tasks, the Jacobian exhibits strong contracting directions near the action endpoint, yet no sampled mode violates the Euler non-expansion condition. On five of those inputs, accuracy sweeps require 4--9 Euler steps at 5% terminal error and 87--112 at 1%. These five paired cases are therefore consistent with accuracy-limited rather than stability-limited sampling under this local criterion, while the controlled experiments show why endpoint accuracy alone cannot rule out a separate stability requirement.

papers.title: ABRR: Transforming Temporal Sentence Grounding with Wasserstein-Adaptive Refinement and Precision Ranking
papers.abstract: Temporal Sentence Grounding (TSG) aims to localize temporal segments in untrimmed videos that correspond to natural language queries, a critical task for video understanding with applications in video retrieval, summarization, and human-computer interaction. Despite significant progress driven by transformer-based models, existing TSG methods suffer from two key limitations: quantization errors due to temporal downsampling, which misalign segment boundaries, and suboptimal ranking of predictions based on semantic matching rather than localization precision. To address these challenges, we propose the Adaptive Boundary Refinement and Ranking (ABRR) framework, a novel, model-agnostic post-processing approach that enhances the performance of any TSG model without retraining. ABRR integrates three innovative components: (1) Temporal Distribution Smoothing, which mitigates noise in predicted score distributions using Gaussian kernel convolution; (2) Boundary Refinement via Optimal Transport, which leverages the 2-Wasserstein distance and Sinkhorn iterations to align coarse segment boundaries with true temporal moments, grounded in Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport theory; and (3) Quality-Driven Re-Ranking, which reorders predictions using a composite score balancing localization precision and semantic relevance. By correcting quantization errors and prioritizing accurately localized segments, ABRR achieves substantial improvements over state-of-the-art TSG models. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including Charades-STA, ActivityNet Captions, and QVHighlights, demonstrate consistent gains at stringent IoU thresholds (e.g., IoU=0.7), alongside enhanced ranking performance. The framework's computational efficiency and compatibility with existing models make it a versatile and impactful solution for real-world TSG applications.

papers.title: PegasusAI Studio: Legible Cyberinfrastructure and Accountable AI Agents for Scientific Workflows
papers.abstract: AI coding agents can now construct scientific workflows, but operating them on shared cyberinfrastructure (CI) raises problems that code generation does not solve. Agents need current knowledge of the workflow system and its execution sites and access to the runtime state of distributed executions, while facilities need to attribute every agent action to a user and bound it by that user's privileges. We present PegasusAI Studio, an AI-assisted science gateway built on the Pegasus and HTCondor stack. Studio makes CI legible to agents by projecting one facility-curated knowledge base into the native configuration of several coding agents, by introspecting workflow interfaces and execution sites, and by grounding diagnosis in workflow and scheduler telemetry. Agent actions operate within a trust envelope that combines federated authentication, per-user execution environments and scheduler credentials, provider-neutral model access, observability, and approval controls for state-changing actions. The same application runs as a JupyterHub-based gateway on a research cloud and as an Open OnDemand application on HPC systems. We evaluate Studio through case studies of legacy CASA weather workflow modernization, a gravitational-wave reanalysis, an EEG analysis built with an open-weight model, and an Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) M87 image reconstruction that recovered from two failed runs to a zero-failure execution. The evaluation establishes that these mechanisms operate as designed.

papers.title: Domain-Adversarial Adaptation from MURA to In-House Radiographs for Improved Adult Elbow Fracture Classification
papers.abstract: We studied domain shift in adult elbow fracture classification from radiographs when training on a large public dataset and deploying on a small, institution-specific dataset (UofL). We implemented a domain-adversarial neural network (DANN) to align feature distributions across source (MURA) and target (UofL) domains while optimizing fracture classification. A pretrained convolutional backbone was adapted to grayscale inputs; the task head predicts fracture presence, and a gradient-reversal-based domain head encourages domain-invariant features via adversarial learning. We compared four settings: (1) Source-only, (2) Target-only (limited labels), (3) Naive merge (pooled training), and (4) DANN (MURA to UofL). Evaluation on UofL test data uses AUC-ROC, and accuracy. DANN outperformed Source-only and Naive merge baselines by reducing domain bias without overfitting to the small target set. Ablations showed that progressive adversarial weight, dataset-size-aware domain loss, and domain-balanced sampling improved stability and target performance. Results demonstrated that domain alignment is a practical path to robust clinical generalization from public to local data.

papers.title: Does Haptic Connection to a Healthy Partner Improve Motor Learning in Chronic Stroke? A Pilot Study of Robot-Based Dyadic Training
papers.abstract: Purpose: Robot-based haptic dyads, where two users exchange forces through robots, have been proposed for robot-assisted neurorehabilitation. This intervention could increase motor learning by promoting motor variability, providing an implicit communication channel, and facilitating social interaction. Despite the potential benefits, few studies have investigated robot-based haptic dyads for neurological populations, and none have included a comprehensive clinical assessment. Design/Methodology/Approach: We present a pilot study investigation of individuals with chronic stroke learning a complex tracking task in solo and dyad conditions. Prior to training, participants completed a battery of cognitive, motor, and sensory assessments. We assessed changes in key kinematic outcomes including tracking error, distance traveled, mean absolute power, and sample entropy. We also performed a correlation analysis of clinical scores with baseline tracking errors. Findings: Baseline tracking error was strongly correlated (r > 0.6) with lower cognitive scores and higher motor scores. Only the solo group demonstrated lower tracking error at assessment (Δ = -5.33, 95%CI [-10.25, -0.40], p = 0.027), but this result was tempered by the removal of an outlier participant. Neither group demonstrated clear retention. The dyad group showed significantly elevated performance, effort, and movement complexity during training. Research Limitations/Implications: The selected task was too difficult to reveal learning for either group, which may be related to its high cognitive demand. Sample size and stroke heterogeneity were also limitation. Originality/Value: Dyadic training increased movement complexity and effort, which are associated with better motor learning. Clinical characteristics such as lesion location, cognition, sensation, and chronicity may influence potential benefits of dyadic training.

papers.title: Train High, Ship Low: Efficient LoRA Synchronization for Distributed On-Policy Post-Training
papers.abstract: Transmitting LoRA adapters to rollout workers can bottleneck distributed on-policy post-training over bandwidth-constrained networks. Lowering the training rank may limit the capacity a workload needs, while adaptive optimizer updates are difficult to compress. Rollout workers can instead reconstruct updates from gradients by maintaining replicated optimizer states. We introduce HiLo, a compressor-agnostic framework that replaces parameter transmission with compressed gradient dissemination and local optimizer replay. By applying the same decoded gradients, the learner and workers maintain consistent policy states at the same version under reproducible execution. We further develop Spar, a budget-aware gradient compressor that combines spectral truncation, adaptive rank allocation and error feedback to decouple training rank from communication cost. Experiments across on-policy distillation and reward-guided post-training show that HiLo with Spar maintains learning quality close to full synchronization while transmitting as little as 1.6% of the adapter bytes, and accelerates end-to-end updates by up to $2.2\times$ under bandwidth constraints.

papers.title: Every hyperbolic knot has an arc-faithful closed braid diagram
papers.abstract: Every hyperbolic knot admits an arc-faithful closed braid diagram, answering Conjecture 29 of McPhail-Snyder. More precisely, any braid representing the knot can be reworded in the same braid group so that the complete holonomy has distinct incoming parabolic fixed points at every crossing. The construction replaces a pinched crossing by five non-pinched crossings when a suitable third strand is adjacent. On $n$ strands it uses at most $2n-1$ letters per replaced crossing. The resulting diagram realizes the complete holonomy by nondegenerate shapes in its four-term octahedral decomposition.

papers.title: DUO: Dual Readouts of Diffusion Models for OOD Detection
papers.abstract: Diffusion models are powerful generative methods for learning and sampling from complex data distributions. Safely deploying these models requires detecting inputs that fall outside their training distribution. Because diffusion models recover clean samples from noisy inputs, reconstruction error is often used for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. This approach assumes that in-distribution (ID) inputs are reconstructed more accurately than OOD inputs. However, OOD inputs may be reconstructed equally well or even better, making this score unreliable. We therefore propose the leading sensitivity spectrum of intermediate denoising features as a complementary OOD signal and demonstrate that it remains informative when reconstruction error is misleading. We introduce DUal-readout of diffusion models for OOD detection (DUO), a fully unsupervised, training-free OOD detector that combines reconstruction error and feature sensitivity. DUO improves average AUROC by approximately 6% points over the strongest baselines while substantially reducing inference cost, and achieves SOTA on near-OOD and high-resolution benchmarks.

papers.title: A Second-Order Parallel Neumann-Robin Splitting for the Stokes-Biot System with a Linear Time-Step Restriction
papers.abstract: In this paper we develop a second-order, fully decoupled, non-iterative partitioned method for the time-dependent Stokes--Biot problem on fixed domains. In previous work \cite{WangLeeCanic2026SecondOrder}, a Robin--Robin scheme with these features was introduced, and its stability and error estimates were established under the sufficient parabolic CFL-type condition $Δt\lesssim C_*h^2$. The main improvement of the new scheme is weakening the CFL-type condition to a linear CFL-type condition $Δt \lesssim C_*h$. This can be achieved with a new splitting approach by replacing the poroelastic mechanical normal Robin condition by its physical Neumann-type traction condition, which results in a Neumann--Robin splitting. For fixed coefficients satisfying the stated assumptions, we prove a fully discrete energy bound under a restriction of $Δt\lesssim C_*h$. The improvement over the parabolic restriction in the earlier Robin--Robin analysis follows from eliminating the interface residual that requires two inverse-trace estimates. We also establish an energy-norm error bound of order $h^k+Δt^2$ under explicit regularity, finite element approximation, and initialization assumptions. Numerical experiments with manufactured solutions examine spatial and temporal accuracy and compare the Neumann--Robin and Robin--Robin schemes. A 3D cylindrical pressure-pulse benchmark further investigates their numerical stability behavior. The results distinguish the less restrictive sufficient stability condition established analytically from the observed stability thresholds of the two schemes.

papers.title: Handlebody-links with Euler characteristic -2 up to six crossings
papers.abstract: We enumerate all non-split handlebody-links with Euler characteristic $-2$ up to six crossings, up to ambient isotopy and mirror image.

papers.title: A Compiler for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) needs compiler intermediate representations (IRs) that preserve error-correcting-code choices, syndrome information, and non-Clifford resource requirements through analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering. We report practical experience building FTQC, an open-source Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect that makes logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames typed static single assignment (SSA) values. Its error-correction-aware type system, two-level lowering design, and IR-resident resource analysis provide one inspectable pipeline to Open Quantum Assembly Language~3 (OpenQASM~3), the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR), Stim, and IQM hardware. Case studies across three code families show that typed metadata makes code-specific decisions verifiable and retargetable: on the 20-qubit Pathfinder at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3 times. They also expose hidden architectural costs: for a three-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT-3), a magic-state factory requires five times the peak qubits of the encoded circuit. These experiences demonstrate a practical foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.

papers.title: Thickness-Field-Excited Bimorph Piezoelectric Micromachined Ultrasonic Transducer in Submicrometer Thin-Film Lithium Niobate
papers.abstract: This work presents the first demonstration of a submicrometer-thick thickness-field-excited (TFE) lithium niobate (LN) flexural-mode piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducer (PMUT). A 670-nm-thick bilayer periodically poled piezoelectric film (P3F) 128Y LN is used to demonstrate a suspended membrane with an area of 0.25 mm$^{2}$, achieving a low resonance frequency of 33.4 kHz for airborne transduction. Its electrical measurements reveal an extracted effective electromechanical coupling efficiency ($k_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}$) of 3% and a moderate static capacitance $C_0$ of 17 pF. Meanwhile, mechanical measurements using a laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV) yield a high quasi-static peak out-of-plane displacement ($ξ_{\mathrm{static}}$) of 145 nm/V and a high corresponding open-circuit sensitivity ($S_{\mathrm{OC}}$) of 1.4 mV/Pa in the audio band. The fabricated device is compared with state-of-the-art (SoA) airborne piezoelectric transducers with sub-100-kHz resonance frequencies, underscoring the potential of the TFE P3F LN transducer platform by simultaneously demonstrating strong actuation capability while featuring high sensitivity.

papers.title: Cryohydrologic Flow and Pingo Formation Within Freezing Impact Melts in Occator Crater, Ceres
papers.abstract: Ceres is a volatile-rich dwarf planet in the asteroid belt and a potential relict ocean world. It exhibits surface features indicative of subsurface brine activity, particularly within Occator Crater. High-resolution imagery from NASA's Dawn Mission reveals landslides, gullies, carbonate faculae, and mound-like features resembling terrestrial pingos on the floor of Occator Crater. Some of these landforms have been hypothesized to form from water, either from the ascent of deep crustal brines or from the freezeout of impact melt. Here, we test the hypothesis that pingo-like features can be formed via the freezing of shallow impact melts. We simulate the heat transfer and groundwater flow dynamics of a freezing impact melt deposit on the floor of Occator Crater. We test a comprehensive parameter space of regolith physical and material properties relevant to the cerean environment. We find that impact melt freezinf produces pressure gradients sufficient to drive hydrologic flow within the melt matrix and could transport fluids to the near surface through hydraulic fracturing. For most of the parameter space tested, water volumes delivered to pingo candidates on the surface meet or exceed those likely required for pingo formation. Analogous hydrologic processes may be important in the shallow subsurface of other regions of Occator Crater and Ceres at large as well as other ice-rich planetary bodies.

papers.title: Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN for Efficient Multipath Parameter Estimation in MIMO Systems
papers.abstract: High-resolution multipath estimation in wideband multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) channels requires repeated searches over angle of arrival, angle of departure, and propagation distance. This paper presents neural network-assisted CLEAN (NN-CLEAN), which replaces the multidimensional search at each extraction step with a multi-head classifier while retaining least-squares (LS) estimation of the complex path gain, parametric reconstruction, and residual cancellation. The same classifier is applied to successive residuals, allowing the extraction depth to vary without changing its output structure. With the number of iterations prescribed by the reference multipath-component (MPC) count, off-grid synthetic tests show that NN-CLEAN slightly exceeds grid-search CLEAN (GS-CLEAN) in path accuracy for one and two MPCs, although its accuracy declines more rapidly at larger path counts. For complete three-MPC extraction at a batch size of eight, NN-CLEAN achieves an approximately $27\times$ speedup and a $52$-fold reduction in peak GPU memory relative to GS-CLEAN. Applied without retraining to two-MPC line-of-sight (LOS) and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) Sionna ray-tracing channels within a coded MIMO link, NN-CLEAN substantially reduces channel-reconstruction mean-squared error (MSE) and bit error rate (BER) relative to interpolated LS channel estimation. GS-CLEAN retains an accuracy advantage on these channels, indicating the estimation cost associated with the computational savings.

papers.title: Domain adaptation of a video Foundation model for Heart Failure Diagnosis from Echocardiography
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of foundation models has transformed computer vision, yet their adaptation to medical imaging, particularly purpose built foundation models for spatio temporal echocardiography videos, remains limited. In this work, we explore the feasibility of fine tuning a pretrained foundation model for video (TimeSformer) for automated diagnosis of reduced ejection fraction heart failure (HFrEF) from apical four chamber videos. The model is finetuned on the publicly available RVENet A4C dataset with a phase aware clip generation strategy that captures complementary systolic and diastolic dynamics. We employ divided space time attention, layer wise learning rate decay, and multi clip inference to enhance robustness under limited data. Experimental results show that full fine tuning of the proposed model outperforms classifier only tuning and a 3D CNN baseline. These findings highlight the potential of leveraging foundation video models for echocardiography based heart failure diagnosis and motivates further domain adaptation studies in medical imaging.

papers.title: A Unified Interactive Framework for Real-Time Three-Dimensional Cellular Automata Simulation in XR
papers.abstract: Integrating three-dimensional cellular automata (3D CA) into extended reality (XR) requires coordinated simulation, volumetric data management, rendering, and interaction under variable hardware constraints. This paper presents a hybrid study combining a critical review of existing approaches with a unified architecture for real-time 3D CA in XR. The proposed five-layer architecture integrates voxel and rule management, parallel computation, interoperability middleware, visualization, and XR interaction. Its key principles include hardware-aware execution, asynchronous simulation-rendering, adaptive fidelity, and cross-engine interoperability. An analytical evaluation framework is defined to assess performance, latency, scalability, memory efficiency, simulation correctness, and interaction quality. The proposed framework provides a foundation for developing portable and interactive 3D CA systems across desktop and mobile XR platforms.

papers.title: Time Series Change Point Detection with Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel general Gaussian process framework for change point detection in time series. A change is defined as an alteration of the hyperparameters of the Gaussian process prior. We formulate the problem in the context of statistical hypothesis testing and demonstrate its performance over both offline and online multiple change points detection. The approach provides theoretical guaranties of its performance. An important advantage of the developed framework is that it does not need a detailed specification of the time series function before and after a change. The hyperparameter values are learned from the data. Comprehensive evaluation of the proposed framework is provided both on synthetic and real data and its efficiency is demonstrated.

papers.title: Function Inversion Reporting
papers.abstract: In the Function Inversion problem, the goal is to invert a function $f:[N] \to [N]$ in two phases. In the preprocessing phase, the offline algorithm computes an advice string of length $S$ bits. In the online phase, the online algorithm receives the advice and a challenge $y \in [N]$, and the goal is to find a preimage $x \in [N]$ such that $f(x) = y$ in time $T$. The problem was initially studied in cryptography, but in recent years it has found various applications to data structure problems. Yet, several of the applications require a variant of Function Inversion, known as Function Inversion Reporting, where the goal is to output all preimages of the challenge $y$. In this paper, we study the Function Inversion Reporting problem in a systematic way by unifying and improving existing algorithms. As a result, we obtain improved data structures for several problems including 3SUM-Indexing Reporting, Range Reporting, Approximate Nearest Neighbor, Jumbled Indexing Reporting, and Gapped String Indexing Reporting.

papers.title: Decode Token Parallelism: Memory-Efficient Distributed Attention Parallelism for Scalable LLM Decoding
papers.abstract: Serving large language models at high concurrency with long contexts requires KV-cache capacity and attention bandwidth that grow with the decode pool. Existing parallelization strategies trade one against the other: data parallelism replicates model weights, limiting KV capacity; tensor parallelism stops scaling attention at the model's KV-head count and pushes dense collectives across nodes; and decode context parallelism (DCP) recovers capacity by sharding the sequence but adds cross-node aggregation of partial attention results. We observe that during decode, dense layers and attention scale differently: dense layers amortize weight reads across the batch and run efficiently within a single NVLink domain, whereas attention cost grows with every active request's KV cache. We present Decode Token Parallelism (TKNP), a decode-pool architecture that decouples weight placement from attention ownership. TKNP distributes a single model copy across nodes in balanced layer blocks. The active node holding a block executes its projections and MLP for the full batch using intra-node tensor parallelism, while every node computes attention for its own requests against locally resident KV cache. This extends request-local attention across nodes without replicating weights: only current-token activations cross the network, dense all-reduces remain within NVLink, and attention requires no cross-node merging of partial results. Implemented in vLLM and evaluated on Llama 3.1 405B and Nemotron-4 340B on up to 64 H100 GPUs, TKNP improves completion throughput for long-context, high-concurrency workloads by up to 1.7$\times$ over DCP and by up to 2.06$\times$ over data parallelism at matched GPU count.

papers.title: Large Language Model Explainability for Planning Lunar Rover Trajectories under Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Planning planetary rover trajectories under probabilistic uncertainty is a multi-objective optimization problem that science teams currently iteratively solve and verify by hand. This process becomes impractical when timelines and constraints frequently shift throughout the mission planning phase. Sampling-based planners such as Monte Carlo tree search can speed up this process, but their outputs do not preserve traceability to the science objectives that justify each plan, which the science team needs to verify. We propose an interactive assistant based on a large language model (LLM) that can explain planner trajectories using domain vocabulary and re-run the planner under user-specified conditions to compare alternatives. Previous work has used LLMs inside planner decision-making loops, but we explore using them for post-planning explanation, where they are more likely to be trusted since they do not directly influence planner decisions. Our framework pairs a simulator inspired by the NASA Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover (VIPER) mission with a ReAct queryable interface that calls curated action tools and retrieval functions. We evaluate the assistant on a query bank consisting of plan comparisons, feasibility, and lookup queries. Experiments show that 90.9% of the assistant's responses are faithful to the planner's outputs, a nearly 65% improvement over zero-shot prompting of the same LLM without tool access, demonstrating the potential for trustworthy explainability of uncertainty-aware traverses with an LLM-based system.

papers.title: Implicit DeepReach Without Implicit Differentiation
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of approximating backward reachable and reach-avoid tubes for high-dimensional nonlinear systems whose Hamiltonians require numerical optimization over constrained controls and disturbances. Existing neural Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability methods alleviate the dimensionality bottleneck of grid-based solvers, but evaluating Hamiltonians without closed-form expressions introduces an additional computational challenge. We show that, under suitable assumptions, the gradients required for value-function training can be computed without differentiating through the inner optimization problem. Specifically, we establish an envelope-type gradient identity for the saddle point Hamiltonian, under which the optimal control and disturbance enter backpropagation as constants without gradient tracking. This enables end-to-end neural HJ reachability with numerically evaluated Hamiltonians while avoiding both solver unrolling and implicit differentiation. We demonstrate the accuracy and computational efficiency of the proposed approach on nonlinear reachability and reach-avoid problems of different scales.

papers.title: Bounded point evaluations in spaces of several complex variables
papers.abstract: The focus of this manuscript is existence criteria for bounded point evaluations and bounded point derivations. In the single variable setting conditions for the existence of bounded point evaluations and derivations are known for many spaces of functions; however, in the several variable case far less is known. In this manuscript, we consider Campanato spaces, which contain many other function spaces as special cases, and prove sufficient conditions for the existence of bounded point evaluations in these spaces that are analogs of known results for the single variable case. We also demonstrate that for certain cases these sufficient conditions are also necessary.

papers.title: MRFoundry: Knowledge-guided agent loops for end-to-end MRI research
papers.abstract: AI agents can write code, use scientific software, and revise computational workflows, opening new possibilities for MRI research. Effective assistance requires connecting acquisition physics, data conventions, specialized tools, and scientific validation. We present MRFoundry, an open-source, extensible package that connects MRI knowledge to agent actions and output checks. Project-local memory preserves decisions and evidence, while reviewed contributions allow researchers to improve shared guidance. Researcher-supervised examples demonstrate skill-guided sequence auditing and acquired-data reconstruction, connecting tool use, output checks, and documented decisions. Alongside MRFoundry, we introduce MRI Agent Bench to compare agents with and without the package across models and MRI task domains. Across 240 paired Core evaluations spanning 24 task types and ten models, all-checks-passed completion increased from 67.5% without MRFoundry to 78.3% with it. Across 134 Hard pairs, completion increased from 36.6% to 44.8%. MRFoundry makes MRI workflow expertise available as reusable guidance that researchers can inspect, adapt, and extend within existing agent and scientific software environments. MRFoundry is openly available at https://github.com/KeWang0622/MRFoundry.

papers.title: A Counterexample to Polynomial Approximation for Monotone Weights
papers.abstract: We give a counterexample to a question of Borichev on polynomial approximation with monotone weights. We construct an even continuous weight $W$, strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$, with superpolynomial growth and finite logarithmic integral, and an entire function $F$ of zero exponential type such that $F/W$ vanishes at infinity and belongs to $L^p(\mathbb{R})$ for every $1\leq p<\infty$. Nevertheless, $F$ has positive distance from the polynomials in the weighted uniform norm and in every corresponding weighted $L^{p}$ norm.

papers.title: Project Progress Desk: Know Where All Your Claude Code and Codex Projects Stand at a Glance
papers.abstract: Codex and Claude Code let developers work on many projects in parallel, but keeping track of them still means switching between chats, terminal sessions and providers. We present Project Progress Desk, a local desktop interface that brings overall progress, blockers and pending decisions into one view. Users can see which projects need attention, inspect what remains, and compare earlier approaches before choosing how to continue. Agent receipts link reported outcomes to each project's weighted acceptance checklist; the overview distinguishes receipt-supported progress from dated estimates. We describe daily use across 36 projects, including a choice between two implementations based on their recorded outcomes. At the demo, attendees will explore 30 simulated projects, trace completed work to overall progress, and watch a coding agent's new result update the overview.

papers.title: Multiple Control Barrier Functions for Geometric Hybrid Systems: Modeling and Safe Control Synthesis
papers.abstract: We formulate geometric hybrid dynamical systems with states on intrinsic manifolds and inputs in topological spaces using relaxed C1-control bundles. Within this framework, we establish a barrier certificate that guarantees forward invariance of a closed set for closed-loop systems. We introduce multiple control barrier functions and derive conditions that render their sublevel sets forward invariant. We then construct pointwise optimal safe control laws, establish regularity conditions for measurable selections, and use these laws to design safety filters for geometric hybrid systems on manifolds. A second-order bouncing-pendulum example illustrates the framework and results.

papers.title: Sharp weighted Riesz inequalities for harmonic mappings in the range 1<p<2
papers.abstract: For $1<p<2$ and $c>0$, we determine the exact norm of the weighted analytic--coanalytic projection operator $F\mapsto(P_+F,\sqrt c\,P_-F)$ from $L^p(\T)$ to $L^p(\T;\ell_2^2)$. The sharp constant is \[ a_{p,c}=\left(\frac{1+c+\sqrt{1+c^2+2c\cos(2π/p)}}{2\sin^2(π/p)}\right)^{1/2}. \] We construct an explicit plurisubharmonic minorant of the corresponding pointwise obstacle and obtain an origin-corrected inequality for arbitrary harmonic decompositions. The uncorrected inequality holds under an optimal angular condition at the origin. The scalar estimate underlying the construction is proved by angular minimization and a two-sided comparison with solutions of $y''=y$. An explicit family establishes sharpness.

papers.title: Closed layers in tensor-triangular geometry
papers.abstract: In the absence of a theory of closed immersions in tensor-triangular geometry, we propose an alternative approach via quotients of module categories. As an application, we prove invariance of homological residue fields under completion.

papers.title: An Accelerated Power Method
papers.abstract: An Accelerated Power Method (APM) for locating the dominant eigen-pair of a real, symmetric matrix is presented. The algorithm is motivated by Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient Method (AGM) and a connection between the APM and the AGM holds, that is analogous to the relationship between the Conjugate Gradient and Lanczos methods. Theoretical convergence analysis shows that the APM is guaranteed to recover the dominant eigen-pair of a normalized semi-definite matrix at a rate no worse than the Power Method. For normalized indefinite matrices, the APM will recover an extremal eigen-pair, but not necessarily the dominant one, and the rate can be worse than the vanilla PM, depending upon the choice of acceleration parameter. Computational practicalities are discussed, including parameter tuning, and numerical experiments are also presented.

papers.title: Network-Co-Designed Dynamic Sparsification for Dependable Distributed Robot Learning over 3GPP Networks
papers.abstract: Robot fleets performing distributed learning often face volatile uplink conditions like bandwidth variation, packet loss, and latency spikes that delay or destabilize training. We propose a network-co-designed dynamic sparsification loop that couples model-update compression to network-facing byte budgets and time constraints. We describe two realizations: (i) a standards-aligned SA6/5GC mapping that leverages CAPIF with NEF/PCF/NWDAF, enriched with AI-specific semantics; and (ii) a VASEAL-style role-reversed loop where the learning system exposes learning-state feedback and receives bounded, time-limited control intents. We implement the mechanism in an asynchronous federated reinforcement learning framework with heterogeneous simulated quadruped robots and reproducible uplink impairments via emulated network links. Results indicate that substantial communication reduction is achievable under dynamic constraints without materially degrading learning progress in the studied setting.

papers.title: Constant query LCCs over the reals
papers.abstract: This note describes a new construction, found by ChatGPT Astra, of constant query Locally Correctable Codes (LCCs) over the real numbers. Prior constructions of constant query LCCs were exclusive to fields of positive characteristic and were conjectured not to exist over the reals. The construction uses low degree polynomial evaluations over an integer grid, together with a novel sampling procedure which outputs, for a given grid point $P$, a random quadratic curve through $P$ which intersects the grid in many other points (the decoding queries). The sampler is `smooth' in the sense that no grid point is queried with high probability. These codes have the additional property that the queried locations (the curve/grid intersections) are all nearby grid points.

papers.title: RetinexGS: Retinex-Inspired Gaussian Splatting for Low-Light RAW Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipelines struggle with severely underexposed images, producing unstable colors, floating artifacts, and incomplete reconstructions in dark regions. To better account for noise in these low-light observations, RAW images offer a natural basis for noise-aware reconstruction by preserving linear sensor measurements and providing access to noise metadata. We present RetinexGS, a RAW-domain 3DGS framework that combines Retinex-inspired appearance modeling with sensor-informed optimization for low-light novel-view synthesis. We factorize each Gaussian's color into a view-independent base color and a shared, position- and view-dependent modulation field, regularizing the two components separately to constrain appearance learning from noisy observations. We use DNG noise metadata to weight the reconstruction loss for signal-dependent noise, while distortion-aware rendering avoids spatially resampling RAW targets. To address sparse geometry in dark regions, we introduce depth-guided initialization. We evaluate RetinexGS on three public RawNeRF scenes and two custom-captured low-light RAW scenes. With all methods trained on the same RAW inputs for each scene, RetinexGS outperforms LE3D and RawNeRF in mean sRGB PSNR by 2.18 dB and 2.71 dB respectively, across the five scenes, while supporting real-time novel-view rendering.

papers.title: Asymptotic Stability of Moving Kinks with an Internal Mode
papers.abstract: We prove asymptotic stability of moving kinks for one-dimensional scalar field equations with one internal mode and no threshold resonance, under a transformed repulsivity condition introduced in Kowalczyk, Martel, Muñoz, and Van Den Bosch and a Fermi golden rule at the second harmonic. Near every fixed subluminal velocity, arbitrary sufficiently small perturbations in $H^1\times L^2$ converge locally in the energy space to a kink with a limiting velocity. The principal difficulty is the coupling between the damping of the internal mode and modulations: the internal oscillation enters the modulation equations quadratically, whereas the damping mechanism provides only quartic time integrability. Inspired by Martel, we derive a velocity normal form from conserved momentum and incorporate the corrected velocity into the virial functional, cancelling the quadratic modulation terms that obstruct the local energy estimates. Matrix Darboux transformations, virial identities at two spatial scales, and a localized Fermi golden rule then yield simultaneous spacetime control of the internal mode and radiation, together with convergence of the velocity. We apply our criterion to the double sine-Gordon equation and suitable perturbations of the $ϕ^4$ model. Through a perturbative analysis of threshold resonances, we determine the full-space discrete spectrum and establish the absence of threshold resonances. We further verify the repulsivity of the twice-transformed potential and the Fermi golden rule.

papers.title: On the number of zeros of polyanalytic polynomials
papers.abstract: We prove that a complex polynomial $f(z,\bar z)$ of degree $n$ in $z$ and degree $m<n$ in $\bar{z}$, with finitely many zeros, has at most $(4m+1)n-5m$ distinct zeros in $\mathbb{C}$. The proof uses an approach suggested by GPT-6.1 based on a topological result of Kronheimer and Mrowka (Thom's Conjecture). We provide examples showing that the bound is asymptotically sharp as $n\to\infty$ for each fixed $m$.

papers.title: Pulsatile Endocrine Regulation with a Releasable Hormone Pool: Impulsive Feedback Model
papers.abstract: An impulsive model of endocrine regulation equipped with frequency- and amplitude-modulated pulsatile feedback is extended to study the dynamical effects pertaining to limitations due to the releasable hormone pool. The model describes a three-hormone regulatory loop and is applicable to endocrine systems such as the reproductive, stress, and growth hormone axes. Conditions guaranteeing the existence and uniqueness of a periodic solution with a single feedback-triggered impulse per period (a 1-cycle) are derived, together with monotonicity properties of its characteristics. An explicit Jacobian formula is obtained to assess local orbital stability. Model analysis demonstrates that a reduced hormone-pool replenishment rate produces a lower-amplitude, higher-frequency 1-cycle. This behavior is consistent with experimentally observed alterations in testosterone regulation in aging human males.

papers.title: An Analytical Model of Compute-limited Multistage Training Pipelines
papers.abstract: Modern foundation models are trained through multiple stages, yet how these stages interact and how compute should be allocated across them remain poorly understood. We introduce an analytically tractable high-dimensional model combining unsupervised pretraining with a linear autoencoder, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with noisy stepwise labels, and reinforcement learning (RL) with sparse episodic rewards. Using random matrix theory and an operator-projection closure, we derive approximate low-dimensional learning dynamics that closely match simulations. We show that finite pretraining data imposes a representation-dependent performance limit, with Bayes classification error scaling as the inverse square root of the pretraining sample ratio, and observe the same exponent in asymptotic SFT and RL errors. Better pretraining also reduces sensitivity to noisy supervision. SFT initialization shortens the initial RL plateau induced by sparse rewards, an effect we also observe in OLMo-2 1B on GSM8K. Longer SFT warm starts additionally improve asymptotic RL performance. Optimizing compute across all three stages reveals that the optimal allocation depends on supervision quality and total budget, with a non-monotonic dependence of the RL compute share on budget. Finally, a complementary compositional model shows how RL selectively strengthens task-relevant pretrained skills while largely preserving unused skills. Together, these results identify mechanisms linking representation quality, feedback structure, and compute allocation in multistage training.

papers.title: Off-policy Learning with Excursion Policies
papers.abstract: Off-policy reinforcement learning (RL) tries to learn the value of a target policy while data comes from a different behavior policy. This often requires trading off bias for variance or stability. One way to trade these off is to linearly interpolate between the behavior and target policies, but this represents only one point in a broader space of interpolation mechanisms. We introduce excursion policies--a structured alternative where the agent follows the target policy for a multi-step "excursion" before reverting to the behavior policy. We derive dynamic programming results for these policies, establishing the theoretical basis for their use in RL. We further develop provably sound off-policy temporal-difference (TD) algorithms for excursion value estimation. We find that excursion policies provide an efficiency-stability trade-off comparable to mixture policies in continuous control benchmarks, and our analysis illustrates conceptual differences in their behavior.

papers.title: On the Chromatic Number of Cayley Tables of Dihedral Groups
papers.abstract: A coloring of a Latin square $L$ is an assignment of $k$ colors to its cells such that no two cells sharing a row, a column, or a symbol receive the same color. The smallest $k$ for which such a coloring exists is called the \emph{chromatic number} of $L$, denoted by $χ(L)$. The Cayley table of a finite group $G$ of order $n$ is a Latin square, which we denote by $L_G$. It is known that $χ(L_G)\ne n+1$, so either $χ(L_G)=n$ or $χ(L_G)\ge n+2$. Moreover, $χ(L_G)=n$ if and only if every Sylow $2$-subgroup of $G$ is trivial or non-cyclic, which completely characterizes the finite groups whose Cayley tables attain the lower bound $n$. In this paper, we consider the dihedral group $D_n$ of order $2n$, where $n$ is odd. Since $D_n$ has a cyclic Sylow $2$-subgroup, it follows that $χ(L_{D_n})\ge 2n+2$. We prove that this bound is sharp, that is, $χ(L_{D_n})=2n+2$.

papers.title: Properties of the Dichromatic Polynomial
papers.abstract: The chromatic polynomial is a well-studied function of graphs whose coefficients, factorization, and other properties are well-known to encode structural information about the underlying graph. An analogous notion of graph colouring exists for directed graphs which is also well-studied, but little is yet known about the corresponding dichromatic polynomial. We investigate properties of the dichromatic polynomial, including its coefficient interpretations, root-dense regions, and asymptotic growth. We also show that chordal digraphs' polynomials split into linear factors in a way analogous to the undirected case, confirm a conjecture on dichromatic uniqueness posed by González-Moreno et al., and study the density of dichromatic polynomials within certain larger families of polynomials.

papers.title: Heterogeneous and episodic permeability evolution and correlation with acoustic emission activity during faulting in granite
papers.abstract: Rock permeability changes dramatically during brittle deformation, affecting faulting dynamics and crustal fluid flow. Here, we combine fluid-flow and local pore-pressure measurements acquired during a quasi-static shear-failure test in Westerly granite with a three-dimensional finite-element inverse method. The measured flow rate and six internal pore pressures constrain the local hydraulic transmissivities (permeability-thickness products) of ten cells along the growing fault. Synthetic ensembles anchored to the pressure-sensor accuracy recover these transmissivities with median mean errors of 7-9%, with the fault ends generally better resolved than the interior. Applied to the experiment, the method resolves episodic transmissivity increases, interspersed with decreases, through fault growth and slip. Local values reach approximately $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ m$^3$ (16 times the bulk contribution), and the final-stage values vary by a factor of 2.3 along the fault. Across cells, the median absolute change in recovered transmissivity is at most about 16% for $\pm50\%$ changes in assumed fault-zone thickness. The local one-dimensional estimates of Aben et al. (2024) agree in scale with the three-dimensional results, with a median 3-D/apparent ratio of 0.81. Cumulative acoustic-emission counts track the overall hydraulic evolution, but the relations of local event density, its stagewise increments and amplitude-weighted activity to transmissivity vary between cells. The comparison distinguishes the value of AE for mapping damage growth from quantitative hydraulic prediction using event-count and relative-amplitude metrics.

papers.title: RaMOD: Moving-Object Detection from Raw mmWave Radar Cubes under Ego Motion
papers.abstract: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar provides weather-robust sensing and direct Doppler measurements, yet automotive perception pipelines often reduce its output to sparse point clouds or two-dimensional projections, leaving raw range-azimuth-Doppler (RAD) cubes underutilized. Ego motion induces Doppler responses from world-static structures, while Doppler wrapping aliases radial velocities, complicating moving-object detection and velocity estimation. We present RaMOD (Radar-based Moving-Object Detection), a real-time framework for moving-object detection and velocity estimation from raw RAD cubes acquired by a vehicle-mounted single-chip radar. RaMOD explicitly estimates frame-wise ego motion and uses the estimated radar translational velocity to predict the Doppler region of world-static structures and suppress returns within it. It temporally encodes the suppressed cubes into multi-scale features to predict RAD-space boxes with class labels. For each detected object, it predicts radial and forward velocities under raw-Doppler and Doppler-unwrapped hypotheses, together with Doppler-wrapping probabilities. On our BRIDGE-Liv dataset, RaMOD outperforms all compared raw-radar methods across RAD-cube, RA, and RD detection settings, achieving 80.8% cube mAP at IoU 0.30, 15.7 percentage points above the strongest RAD-cube baseline. Velocity MAE is 1.128 m/s, with 99.87% Doppler-wrapping accuracy.

papers.title: What drives the emergence of symbolic mechanisms in large language models?
papers.abstract: Recent work has identified a set of emergent symbolic mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in large language models, but it remains unclear what factors drive the emergence of these mechanisms. To address this question, we trained neural networks from scratch on abstract sequence tasks, varying both architectural and data distributional factors, and investigated the effects of these factors on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms. Using representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses, we first confirmed that transformer-based language models trained from scratch on our task developed symbolic mechanisms. We then found that, across multiple axes of data diversity, greater diversity produced stronger symbolic signatures. Surprisingly, the same signatures emerged in modified transformer architectures and even multilayer perceptrons, indicating that architectural inductive biases are not necessary for the development of symbolic mechanisms. We also observed consistent patterns in an entity-attribute binding task. Together, these findings identify data diversity, not architecture, as the primary driver of emergent symbolic computation in neural networks.

papers.title: Viscosity heats, diffusion drains: Open-system thermodynamics in unimodular cosmology
papers.abstract: In GR with bulk viscosity and in unimodular gravity with energy diffusion, the matter sector is non-adiabatic, and their balance, entropy, and temperature equations match if $Π\leftrightarrow \dot{Q}/3H$. Disagreement over whether unimodular cosmology is adiabatic comes from assigning entropy to matter only or to the total effective fluid. The key is the temperature $T_D$ of the sector absorbing the diffused energy: comoving entropy production is $\dot{Q}(1/T_D-1/T_m)$, yielding earlier limits for $T_D \rightarrow \infty$ and $T_D \rightarrow T_m$. For finite $T_D$, diffusion acts like heat exchange with an external reservoir: unlike viscosity, which only heats a closed fluid, diffusion into a colder bath can cool an open one, breaking the viscosity-diffusion correspondence for observables and stability. Cosmographically, $Π$ is fixed by the deceleration $q$, while diffusion is fixed by the jerk $j$; thus $Λ$CDM is the adiabatic limit of unimodular cosmology but remains dissipative when modeled via viscosity. The diffusive analogue of $|Π|/ρ$ is the shift $c_s^2-ω$ in effective sound speed, set by perturbative stability rather than acceleration. If dark matter is a gas with conserved rest mass, consistent diffusion removes only thermal energy, forbids phantom behavior, and bounds the growth of the cosmological term by the finite thermal reservoir; producing a logotropic dark fluid with conserved particle number would require relativistic dark matter at $z\simeq12$. With the Hayward-Kodama apparent-horizon temperature, the generalized second law in unimodular gravity follows from the local one, whereas for bulk viscosity it must be imposed separately.

papers.title: Force-Closure Condition for Cooperative Multi-robot Pushing of Rectangular Objects
papers.abstract: In cooperative object manipulation, the placement of pushing contacts determines whether force closure can be achieved and agents can generate arbitrary forces and torques on the object correspondingly. This study derives a necessary and sufficient closed-form condition for the planar force closure of a rectangular object, a common object shape in everyday settings, under four frictionless pushing contacts. For a rectangle of length $b$ and width $a$, force closure holds if and only if $(l_1+l_3-b)(l_2+l_4-a)<0$, where $l_1,l_2,l_3,l_4$ are the four edge contact locations. This condition is independent of the object's center of mass and is used to verify contact configurations before contact force allocation. When the condition is not satisfied, the signs of the two factors indicate which opposing contact pair should be adjusted. The condition and adjustment rule are then integrated into a full-pose trajectory-tracking framework as a geometric feasibility layer to demonstrate their use in control. Static wrench feasibility tests validate the proposed condition, while narrow-passage floating-body simulations show that maintaining a force-closure configuration reduces the RMS tracking errors in $x$, $y$, and unwrapped yaw from $12.05$ m, $18.11$ m, and $535.96^\circ$ to $2.24$ m, $2.66$ m, and $2.69^\circ$, respectively.

papers.title: The Cayley-Bedregal reduction for Milnor and Hirzebruch-Milnor classes
papers.abstract: The Cayley--Bedregal reduction replaces a complete intersection $\{f_1=\dots=f_r=0\}$ by the hypersurface $\sum_iφ_if_i=0$ in the projectivized dual bundle. For an isolated complete intersection singularity of corank $c$, we express the Milnor class of this hypersurface on its singular fibre $\mathbb P^{c-1}$ in terms of the Milnor numbers of generic systems obtained by taking linear combinations of the defining equations. Its degree is the original Milnor number, and the higher components recover the Milnor numbers of the systems with fewer equations. These numbers are invariants of the analytic germ. Our second main result concerns the Hodge-theoretic refinement. For a complete intersection defined by a regular section of a rank-$r$ algebraic vector bundle, the Hirzebruch--Milnor class is determined by that of the Cayley--Bedregal hypersurface: the push-forward of the normalized Hirzebruch--Milnor class of the hypersurface, in the sense of Cappell, Maxim, Schürmann and Shaneson, is $(-y)^{r-1}$ times that of the complete intersection, with no positivity assumption on the bundle. The factor $(-y)^{r-1}$ comes from the motivic decomposition of the projective bundle, and at $y=-1$ the identity recovers Aluffi's comparison of Milnor classes. When the tautological bundle is very ample, the hypersurface formula of Maxim, Saito and Schürmann then gives the Hirzebruch--Milnor class of the complete intersection through the vanishing cycles of a single function, avoiding their induction through intermediate complete intersections and their restriction to powers of one line bundle. In integral homology we prove the analytic form of Aluffi's identity, and obtain formulas for the Milnor class in terms of local Milnor fibres and for the Chern--Schwartz--MacPherson class of any projective scheme.

papers.title: Challenging the hoop conjecture with spinning pancakes and baguettes
papers.abstract: Understanding when gravitational collapse produces a black hole remains a central challenge in general relativity. Black-hole uniqueness results characterize the stationary endpoint under suitable assumptions, while singularity theorems establish geodesic incompleteness in the presence of trapped surfaces and appropriate energy and global conditions. Neither, however, provides a general criterion for horizon formation. The hoop conjecture offers such a criterion by relating the enclosed mass to the compactness of a matter distribution in every direction. We construct axisymmetric families of initial data describing rotating dust and test a formulation of the conjecture adapted to this setting. We explore highly prolate and oblate configurations with both constant and differential rescaled angular-velocity profiles, including configurations near the threshold for apparent-horizon formation. We find that the conjecture holds for rotating configurations, with a coefficient within 14% of unity as in the nonrotating case, provided the quasilocal mass includes the rotational energy. If the irreducible mass of the apparent horizon is used instead, the deviations grow with spin, as they do for Kerr black holes. For horizonless configurations, the conjecture likewise holds when the mass is restricted to the energy enclosed by the matter surface, whereas using the ADM mass, which also includes rotational field energy outside the matter, leads to apparent violations of up to $\approx$25%. We also discuss the possible evolution of compact configurations without apparent horizons, their relation to weak cosmic censorship, and their implications for horizonless compact objects.

papers.title: Effect of car-centric social norms on traffic congestion in a compartmental model of transit mode utilization
papers.abstract: Vehicle traffic congestion is a persistent feature of urban transportation systems around the world.Importantly, congestion is in part a consequence of human decision-making: car traffic is reduced when people choose modes of transportation such as metro trains, buses, or trams, over cars, and it is amplified when there is a persistent social bias towards driving. The underlying feedback loop in which traffic levels influence transportation mode choices, which in turn affect traffic levels themselves, is poorly understood and we study its consequences in the presented work using a compartmental modeling approach. We first consider a simplified model of only car traffic and show that it predicts a hysteresis between congested and uncongested states, which is consistent with broader literature on on traffic modeling. Next, we add buses and trains to the model as alternative transit modes, confirm the existence of hysteresis in this generalization, and derive the relative trip completion rates of each mode. Finally, to account for decision-making, we take the demand rates for the different transit modes to be dynamic, closing the feedback loop between mode choice and utilization. This redistributes demand for each mode of transportation, highlighting that traffic conditions may be a key aspect of mode choice. Furthermore, our model predicts that increasing public awareness of congestion can be an effective control strategy to increase utilization of public transit. However, car-centric social norms must be sufficiently small, or car use is instead amplified.

papers.title: Hybridization-brightened interlayer excitons in multilayer WSe2 controlled by sliding ferroelectricity
papers.abstract: Interlayer excitons (IXs) combine spatially separated electron and hole wavefunctions with electrically tunable dipole moments, but their reduced wavefunction overlap generally limits optical emission, particularly for high-energy states. Here we report a bright, spectrally narrow high-energy interlayer exciton (h-IX) near 2.23 eV in few-layer WSe2 and investigate how its optical activity evolves with layer number and sliding-ferroelectric polarization. In pristine 2H-WSe2, we observe thickness-dependent brightening of high-energy exciton emission. GW-BSE calculations reveal mixed intralayer and interlayer configurations with enhanced optical weight, suggesting that multilayer hybridization contributes to the observed brightening. In parallel-stacked 3L/3L WSe2 containing a sliding-ferroelectric interface, the h-IX exhibits polarization-dependent energies and Stark responses that distinguish Pup and Pdown domains. Electric-field-driven domain-wall motion produces hysteretic transfer of spectral weight between the two h-IX branches, enabling optical tracking of ferroelectric switching. These results establish multilayer hybridization as a route to optically active high-energy interlayer excitons and sliding ferroelectricity as a complementary degree of freedom for controlling their energy, dipole and emission.

papers.title: Global regularity of axisymmetric Navier--Stokes equations under total slip and critical smallness
papers.abstract: We study the axisymmetric incompressible Navier--Stokes equations in a finite cylinder subject to the Navier--total--slip boundary condition, that is, the Navier slip condition with zero friction. We prove that the solution remains smooth for all time provided that the initial swirl $Γ_0 = r v_{θ,0}$ has zero mean and an explicit smallness condition on the initial data holds. The condition involves $Γ= rv_θ$ and the variables $V = v_θ/\sqrt{r}$ and $Ω= ω_θ/r$, and it is invariant under the natural scaling of the Navier--Stokes equations, hence critical. The total-slip condition produces a boundary term on the lateral wall that cannot be controlled by the dissipation alone; we overcome this with a sharp trace-type identity combined with a remainder controlled by $\|Γ\|_{L^2}$. In addition, the Robin-type boundary condition $\partial_r Γ= 2Γ$ destroys the maximum principle for $Γ$, and we replace it with a uniform $L^4$ bound. These estimates yield uniform $L^4$ bounds for the velocity, and regularity follows from the Ladyzhenskaya--Prodi--Serrin criterion together with boundary regularity results for the Navier slip condition.

papers.title: Adaptive Residual Quantization for Memory-Efficient Temporal Action Segmentation
papers.abstract: Temporal action segmentation (TAS) is commonly trained on large banks of pre-extracted frame features, but storing and replaying those features becomes a practical bottleneck for long-form video, especially in incremental TAS where past-task data must remain available to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. Recent TAS replay and condensation methods reduce this burden, but they rely on dense frame-wise annotations and allocate storage through fixed segment-level structures, limiting their flexibility for long procedural videos whose frame complexity varies substantially over time. We introduce Adaptive Residual-Quantized Variational AutoEncoder (ARQ-VAE), a compact and label-free memory representation for TAS features that learns a discrete residual quantization of frame-level video features and then adaptively truncates the residual chain on a per-frame basis, retaining only the residual prefix that best reconstructs each frame feature. This yields a practical compact feature memory that does not depend on frame-wise labels and can therefore support multiple TAS settings with the same stored representation, while a lightweight fine-tuning stage further improves reconstruction quality for the truncated codes that are actually retained. Across standard TAS benchmarks, ARQ-VAE achieves a substantially improved storage-performance trade-off over prior replay and condensation baselines. On Breakfast, our final representation reduces training-set storage from 28 GB for the original I3D feature bank to 10 MB while retaining strong downstream segmentation performance; with ASFormer, it achieves 71.5 Edit and 51.2 F1@50 in the supervised setting. We further show that the same label-free memory remains effective for incremental and unsupervised TAS. We position ARQ-VAE as a practical memory representation for TAS and a promising direction for broader dataset condensation applications.

papers.title: Expiscating the black hole singularity in holography
papers.abstract: We argue that the leading exponential rate in the high frequency asymptotics of holographic thermal two-point functions is independent of the conformal dimension and spin (held fixed) of the operator. We analyze the leading universal WKB spectral curve governing the asymptotics at non-vanishing momentum scaling with frequency. We show that its classical action governs time domain signatures of the bouncing geodesic singularity, highly damped quasinormal modes, and the asymptotics of multi-stress tensor OPE coefficients. Beyond the leading order, we examine linear and dimension-dependent sublinear scalings of momentum with frequency. In both regimes, we derive the connection matrix between the boundary and the horizon using exact-WKB techniques. The results show a factorization of the spectral function into a perturbative part controlled by the OPE and a non-perturbative part governed by WKB transport. For linear scaling at fixed $k/ω$ in the timelike regime, the turning points controlling physical transport remain separated from the curvature singularity. Nevertheless, a singularity-anchored representative of the same transport homology class determines the leading WKB action. In the sublinear regime, the relevant turning points approach the singularity. We match an exact solution of the near-singularity scaled equation to the exterior WKB solution to determine the connection matrix and spectral function. Our results clarify how the black hole curvature singularity is encoded in dual field theory observables at leading order in the planar expansion.

papers.title: Beyond the Fast Rotators: A JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury Survey of Substellar Weather
papers.abstract: Atmospheric variability provides a unique window into the three-dimensional structure, dynamics, and evolution of brown dwarf and giant exoplanet atmospheres. Recent JWST time-resolved spectroscopic observations have revealed complex wavelength-dependent variability, offering unprecedented insights into cloud structures, thermal perturbations, and atmospheric chemistry. However, existing programs have focused primarily on individual benchmarks and specific scientific questions, resulting in heterogeneous spectral and temporal coverage and leaving important regions of the substellar population underexplored, particularly across a broad range of rotation periods, spectral types, and viewing geometries. A JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury program could systematically investigate substellar weather across a diverse, well-characterized population. By combining broad infrared spectroscopic coverage with observations spanning multiple rotations and strategically selected epochs, this program would constrain the contributions of different physical mechanisms while investigating how atmospheric structures depend on rotation, viewing geometry, and fundamental physical properties. Extended monitoring would also improve rotational-period determinations and reveal how atmospheric features evolve from rotation to rotation and over longer timescales. This coordinated effort would provide a consistently designed and uniformly processed dataset of time-resolved spectra and variability diagnostics, enabling population-level comparisons, testing predictions from three-dimensional circulation models, and establishing a framework for interpreting the atmospheric diversity and evolution of brown dwarfs and directly imaged giant exoplanets.

papers.title: Choosing Complexity: Cognitive Ability, Overconfidence, and Task Choice
papers.abstract: Workers and organizations routinely choose between complex tasks that differ in their success-payment tradeoff. We study how cognitive ability and overconfidence shape this choice of task complexity, both theoretically and experimentally. Consistent with our model, we find that more cognitively able individuals choose more complex tasks. Conditional on cognitive ability, we find that more overconfident individuals also choose more complex tasks. In about 75% of the decisions, subjects pick their payoff-maximizing task, and higher cognitive ability is weakly associated with more efficient choices of task complexity. But errors are strikingly one-sided: those who fail to choose optimally pick tasks that are too complex. Our findings suggest that organizations should pair task menus and incentives for choosing more complex tasks with information and feedback that help workers assess their ability and probability of success.
